items.title: Hashing vs encryption vs encoding
items.body: Hashing is one-way and keyless; encryption is reversible with a key; encoding such as Base64 is reversible by anyone and provides no secrecy. Store passwords with a password hash, never with reversible encryption.

items.title: Password hashing with Argon2id or bcrypt
items.body: Password hashes must be salted and deliberately slow so offline guessing is expensive. OWASP recommends Argon2id (for example 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, parallelism 1), then scrypt, with bcrypt for legacy systems. Fast hashes like SHA-256 allow billions of GPU guesses per second.
items.question: What bcrypt limitation should you know before hashing long passphrases?
items.answer: bcrypt only uses the first 72 bytes of input, so longer passwords are silently truncated. Prefer Argon2id, and avoid naive pre-hashing that can introduce null bytes.

items.title: Reusing an AES-GCM nonce
items.question: A service encrypts records with AES-GCM using one key and a counter nonce that resets to zero on every restart. How bad is that?
items.answer: Catastrophic. Reusing a nonce with the same key reveals the XOR of the two plaintexts and lets an attacker recover the authentication key and forge valid ciphertexts. Use random 96-bit nonces with key rotation well before about 2^32 messages, a persistent counter, or a nonce-misuse-resistant mode like AES-GCM-SIV.

items.title: Comparing webhook signatures
items.question: Your webhook handler computes an HMAC and checks it with signature == expected. A reviewer flags it. Why, and what is the fix?
items.answer: Ordinary string comparison returns at the first differing byte, so response timing can leak how much of a guess is correct. Compare with a constant-time function such as crypto.timingSafeEqual in Node or hmac.compare_digest in Python, after checking the lengths match.

items.title: Why HMAC instead of hash(secret + msg)
items.question: Why is sha256(secret + message) a bad way to authenticate a message?
items.answer: SHA-256 is a Merkle-Damgard hash, so from a valid digest an attacker can compute the hash of message plus padding plus extra data without knowing the secret: a length extension attack. HMAC nests two keyed hashes and is not vulnerable, so use HMAC-SHA256.

items.title: Use a CSPRNG for secrets
items.body: Tokens, keys, nonces and reset codes must come from a cryptographically secure generator such as crypto.getRandomValues, crypto.randomBytes or Python secrets. Math.random and similar PRNGs are predictable from their outputs.
